title: Supervised vs Self-Supervised Learning on Audio
text: This research project compared supervised and self-supervised machine learning approaches on music and speech classification tasks. Supervised models learn with labeled data, while self-supervised models learn with unlabeled data. The goal was to understand how deep neural networks organize information internally in their intermediate layers, and whether self-supervised models show signs of task specialization (models that show signs of processing speech/music tasks differently imitate how the brain’s auditory cortex works).

title: Supervised vs Self-Supervised Learning on Audio
text: This research project compared supervised and self-supervised machine learning approaches on music and speech classification tasks. Supervised models learn with labeled data, while self-supervised models learn with unlabeled data. The goal was to understand how deep neural networks organize information internally in their intermediate layers, and whether self-supervised models show signs of task specialization (models that show signs of processing speech/music tasks differently imitate how the brain’s auditory cortex works).

title: Supervised vs Self-Supervised Learning on Audio
text:
Methods

Models: PaSST (supervised) and BYOL-A (self-supervised)
Data: Google Speech Commands dataset, Free Music Archive, DCASE environmental noise
Input: Log-mel spectrograms (time-frequency audio representations)
Analysis: Extracted embeddings from final and intermediate layers (13-14 layers for each model) to visualize how models represent speech vs. music

title: Supervised vs Self-Supervised Learning on Audio

PaSST outperformed BYOL-A on classification accuracy. However, BYOL-A showed significant layer-wise task specialization—early layers clearly separated speech from music processing, while PaSST’s intermediate layers formed no distinct clusters.
This suggests that supervised models are more prone to having a higher accuracy since they train on labeled data, while self-supervised models develop representations that may mirror brain processing.

title: Block Museum Calendar Automation
text: The Block Museum at Northwestern maintains weekly calendar archives documenting events and attendance. Creating these archives used to involve time-intensive manual editing: exporting Outlook calendars to PDF, manually transcribing event details into a Word template, and correcting data-entry mistakes. This project automated the entire pipeline with a Python application + Power Automate workflow.

title: Block Museum Calendar Automation
text: The Block Museum at Northwestern maintains weekly calendar archives documenting events and attendance. Creating these archives used to involve time-intensive manual editing: exporting Outlook calendars to PDF, manually transcribing event details into a Word template, and correcting data-entry mistakes. This project automated the entire pipeline with a Python application + Power Automate workflow.

title: Block Museum Calendar Automation
text:
Implementation
The calendar archival undergoes the following steps: 1. Power Automate exports Outlook calendar to customized CSVs weekly and sends an email to employees when it is exported - Both manual and automatic Power Automate flows created for employees’ convenience 2. The Python script (block_converter.exe) reads CSV, cleans data, and generates a formatted Word document - Filters exclude unnecessary events (“CANCELED”, “OOO”, “AUTOMATED” entries) - Events descriptions are validated to ensure they follow the museum’s Required Fields Template - Creates a formatted Word document (python-docx) with proper fonts, spacing, indentation 3. One-click output uploads formatted .docx file to SharePoint

title: Audio Description Selection
text:
Audio descriptions (AD) narrate visual events in video for blind and low vision audiences. With open-source AD generation models now being available, the challenge is selecting the best candidate description from a pool. This project explored whether lightweight supervised ML models can automatically select high-quality AI-generated ADs using only textual features.
Video demo: compares ground truth human-written audio description, “GT AD”, vs. AI-generated audio description, “AI AD”. Shows the lightweight selector model I built working on TV scenes.

title: Audio Description Selection
text:
Audio descriptions (AD) narrate visual events in video for blind and low vision audiences. With open-source AD generation models now being available, the challenge is selecting the best candidate description from a pool. This project explored whether lightweight supervised ML models can automatically select high-quality AI-generated ADs using only textual features.
Video demo: compares ground truth human-written audio description, “GT AD”, vs. AI-generated audio description, “AI AD”. Shows the lightweight selector model I built working on TV scenes.

title: Audio Description Selection
text:
Methods

Generated 5 candidate ADs per scene across 2,983 TV scenes (Friends, The Big Bang Theory) using Qwen2-VL-7B (VLM) and LLaMA-3-8B (LLM) on a HPCC
Extracted 9 textual features from each candidate: token count, action verb density, pronoun ratios, type-token ratio, consensus score, etc.
Trained classification and regression models (logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost) with 5-fold cross-validation
Evaluated two quality metrics as response variables: embedding similarity (Q1) and action score matching (Q2)

Logistic regression achieved 33.7% accuracy on action score selection, which is a 13.6 percentage point improvement over a baseline of random selection. The most important features were action verb count, pronoun-to-noun ratio, and consensus score. More details about these features are available in the code repository.
